abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: While topological effects have proven fruitful in quantum and classical wave systems, their application in diffusion encounters challenges. The dissipative nature of thermal diffusion poses a difficulty in achieving stably existing eigenstates at real frequencies, thus limiting the realization of robust topological states of heat. This study introduces a strategy for designing diffusion systems to behave just like wave systems. By introducing an additional periodic dimension, we provide a degree of freedom that enables the system eigenvalues to transition from “imaginary” to “real.” This approach facilitates the establishment of counterparts of various topological lattices in diffusion systems, extending the benefits of topology to diffusion processes and contributing to dynamic heat control.

sec.p: Keywords: topological modes, delocalization, thermal lattice, wave-like heat transfer

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The topological physics has sparked intensive investigations into topological lattices in photonic, acoustic, and mechanical systems, powering counterintuitive effects otherwise inaccessible with usual settings. Following the success of these endeavors in classical wave dynamics, there has been a growing interest in establishing their topological counterparts in diffusion. Here, we propose an additional real-space dimension in diffusion, and the system eigenvalues are transformed from “imaginary” to “real.” By judiciously tailoring the effective Hamiltonian with coupling networks, localized and delocalized topological modes are realized in heat transfer. Simulations and experiments in active thermal lattices validate the effectiveness of the proposed theoretical strategy. This approach can be applied to establish various topological lattices in diffusion systems, offering insights into engineering topologically protected edge states in dynamic diffusive scenarios.

sec.p: Received 2024 May 3; Accepted 2024 Jul 21; Issue date 2024 Aug 27.

body.p: Classical wave systems borrow concepts well established in condensed matter systems, showcasing fruitful achievements (1, 2) by tailoring system coupling interactions to construct an analogy to the Hamiltonian in quantum physics. Establishing systems from the view of the eigenstate-based band theory enables special phenomena not available in natural materials and offers effective ways to control the wave propagation. Representative examples include phononic and photonic crystals (3) with designed band structures, as well as the emerging topological insulators in mechanics (4), acoustics (5) and photonics (6, 7). Based on engineering the eigenenergy or eigenfrequency band, developments in topological systems with in-gap edge states have drawn considerable interest due to the enhanced robust performance of physical systems. The existence of these topologically protected edge states is fully determined by the system’s topological properties, exhibiting robustness against perturbations and immunity to defects (8, 9). Yet almost all profound conclusions are in the framework of wave systems. Because one of the prerequisites for these successes is the formal similarity between classical wave equation and Schrodinger equation. Usually for closed systems where energy or probability are conserved, the Hermiticity of their Hamiltonian guarantees the real eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenstates of stable existence. However, it is difficult for the diffusion system to take advantage of this kind of robustness, for diffusive systems are anti-Hermitian (10) with intrinsic dissipative nature. Due to the inherent limitations of the diffusion field, in most existing explorations (11–14) on thermal topology, the energy band is opened in the imaginary part of the frequency domain. The edge state emerges as a mode undergoing attenuation at an in-gap decay rate, through a dissipation process from an initial specific distribution to a final uniform state. As a result, thermal topological phenomena appear to deviate significantly from those observed in traditional wave topology. This gap reveals that continuing with previous frameworks and relying solely on spontaneous diffusion terms for coupling may consistently fail to produce the expected well-known topological behaviors.

To overcome this limitation, here we propose a strategy to design diffusion systems with mathematical structures equivalent to wave systems. The conversion from “anti-Hermitian” to “Hermitian-like” is realized by engineering the couplings within an additionally introduced dimension. Based on the proposed paradigm, we construct the counterparts of SSH/quadrupole model in thermal regime and find a topological zero mode located at the edge/corner within the eigenfrequency gap. We further obtain the complete delocalization (15, 16) of the topological mode by introducing non-Hermiticity (17) into the effective Hamiltonian. The theoretical strategy is verified with simulations and proof-of-principal experiments in programmable thermal lattices. Our findings provide inspiration for building dynamically stable diffusion systems with characteristics like wave dynamics, which are also beneficial to a wide variety of topological applications in diffusive contexts (18, 19).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We first start with the similarities and differences on the physical governing equations between the wave and diffusion systems. Usually for wave dynamics, a wave field Ψ satisfies the wave equation ∂2tΨ=a2∇2Ψ, where a is a real number that reflects the propagation speed of the wave (Fig. 1A). In terms of diffusion (20–22), a potential field Ψ is governed by ∂tΨ=D∇2Ψ, where D represents the diffusivity. We see that the second-order time derivative in the wave equation is changed to a first-order time derivative in diffusion, making the diffusive potential field lose the propagation property and exhibit absolute in situ decay (Fig. 1B). As many advances in classical physical systems have been inspired by the concepts in quantum physics (23), the equations can be reviewed in the form of the Schrodinger equation: i∂tΨ=HΨ, where H is the Hamiltonian and the eigenfield takes the form of plane wave solution Ψ=eikx-iωt. For closed wave systems, their mathematical structures are built on Hermitian operators satisfying H=H†, guaranteeing the real eigenvalues that represent the wave frequency. While diffusive systems are naturally open systems with anti-Hermitian Hamiltonian satisfying H=-H†, the eigenvalues are pure imaginary numbers whose modulus corresponds to the decay rate. Now that the eigenvalues of these two systems differ by a factor of the imaginary unit i, it is intriguing and interesting to wonder whether we can convert the two sorts of systems to one another, e.g., constructing a diffusion system that allows traveling wave transportation like a wave system. If successful, those topological phenomena that have been observed in quantum and classical systems can also be explored in diffusion systems for the benefit of robust transport of heat or mass.

caption.p: Engineering a diffusion system with pure real eigenvalues. (A and B) Characteristics of wave dynamics (A) and diffusion (B). Eigenvalues of a wave/diffusion system are real/imaginary due to the intrinsic governing equations. (C and D) The strategy of constructing a diffusion system (D) with eigenspectra mathematically equivalent to a wave system (C). An additional dimension labeled as s is introduced in the diffusion system, where the designed hopping relationship causes the effective Hamiltonian to incorporate a factor of the imaginary unit i, transforming the system eigenvalues from imaginary to real. (E) The spectra of a 1D SSH chain for a wave system, where the staggered hopping opens a gap in bulk momentum space (PBC). (F) The spectra of the chain with an additional dimension s in the context of diffusion. The eigenvalues are all real numbers. The graph at the cross section for a specific ks is identical with (E) under both PBC and OBC (in the x direction), confirming the equivalence of the two systems.

sec.p: We propose a scheme to equivalently realize this desired prospect, as illustrated in Fig. 1 C and D. Considering a one-dimensional lattice in the case of wave dynamics, we focus on the couplings between the site II and its two nearest neighbors I and III, as shown in highlighted color in Fig. 1C. The equation related with the eigenvalue ω satisfies i∂tΨ=HΨ=ωΨ, with Ψ=⋯,AI,AII,AIII,⋯Te-iωt and A∗ represents the wavefunction components at each site. Then we introduce the lattice structure with asymmetric hoppings in an extra dimension denoted by s-axis in Fig. 1D. J is the total number of sites in the s-direction, and j = 1,2…,J represents the index of sublattice. The characteristic equation turns to be

Given periodic (Born-von Karman) boundary condition (PBC) in the s-direction, ks is a good quantum number. It guarantees A∗,j=A∗eiksj, where the wavenumber ks is chosen to take on values from the first Brillouin zone (ks=2πn/J with n=1,⋯,J). Reframing Eq. 2 by treating each set of all the sublattice sites along the s-axis as a single unit and concentrating on the effective hoppings among these units yields:
Comparing Eq. 3 with Eq. 1, we find that they are almost identical, except that the left-hand side of Eq. 3 acquires a factor of -i, and the effective terms can be calculated by

where χ stands for the hopping parameters v, w, and ω0. It is a result of the designed coupling relationships through the s-dimension. With fixed ks, the factor i can serve as a bridge for transforming the system eigenvalues between real and imaginary. As mentioned earlier, the eigenvalues of a diffusion system differ from those of a wave system by i. Therefore, diffusion systems employing the lattice in Fig. 1D will share the same effective mathematical structure with Fig. 1C in wave systems and exhibit a wave-like performance.

Moreover, the lattice can be designed with a tailorable band structure at real frequency by tuning the hopping amplitudes. Taking the well-known Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) model (24) as an example, the staggered hopping opens a gap in bulk momentum space, see Fig. 1E. In the topologically non-trivial case (intracell hopping v′ < intercell hopping w′), the bulk-boundary correspondence predicts the existence of zero-energy states exponentially localized at the left/right edge under open boundary condition (OBC). We replicate this model in a diffusion system by adding an extra s dimension and plot the eigenvalues in Fig. 1F. Simply focusing on the cross section at a specific wavenumber ks, the graph can be identical to that in Fig. 1E, as long as the parameters satisfy Eq. 4. It confirms the equivalence of the two systems at a given wavenumber ks. Note that the introduced s-dimension is “suppressed” and solely responsible for turning the imaginary eigenvalues into real ones. Thus, we designate the lattice organized as Fig. 1D as Quasi-1D lattices, despite the physical real space appearing two-dimensional. For results in Fig. 1 E and F, the lattice structures are depicted in the subfigures at the bottom, where the green box encloses the unit cell. The chain has 20 sites in the x direction, with v = 1, w = 4, v′ = 2sin ks·v, w′ = 2sin ks·w and ks = 2 π/3.

Using the proposed design principle, we can construct various thermal lattices that support topological modes in the form of dynamic wave-like heat transfer, particularly focusing on the localization and delocalization of topological edge states in non-Hermitian systems. Non-Hermiticity has emerged as a recent solution to address the low bulk utilization of bulky and costly lattices, providing a powerful degree of freedom for tailoring topological wavefunctions at will (25), spanning mechanical (26), acoustic (27) and circuit (28) systems. Especially, a recent experiment (15) presents remarkable results on using the non-Hermitian skin effect to reshape the spatial distribution of topological states. In the following, we will introduce how it can be used in thermal systems.
The non-Hermitian SSH (NH-SSH) chain is displayed in Fig. 2A, whose bulk Hamiltonian is written as:

sec.p: where the intracell hoppings v1′ and v2′ are non-reciprocal. Different from the Hermitian SSH (H-SSH) case, the energy spectrum under PBC becomes complex (29), forming a loop on the complex plane as kx varies from 0 to 2 π, see Fig. 2B. The topological properties are determined by the non-Bloch winding number in a generalized Brillouin zone (30) and the topological transition occurs at v′1v′2=w′. Here the coupling coefficients are set as: w0′ = 0, v1′ = 1 and w′ = 4, and for all v2′ in Fig. 3 B and C, the chain remains topologically non-trivial (v′1v′2=w′), as indicated by the topological modes pinned at zero energy under OBC. However, with the increase of v2′, the wavefunctions of the topological zero modes transition from being localized at the left end to being localized at the right, passing through a critical value (v2′ = w′) where the extended mode occurs (Fig. 3C). At this critical value, also called Bloch points (31, 32), the mode restores a Bloch-wave-like profile, achieving a balance between the localization effect and the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE). It presents as an eigenfield extended into the bulk while the eigenvalue remains spectrally isolated in the bandgap with intact topological protections.

caption.p: Experimental observation of topological modes in a thermal lattice. (A) The quasi-1D thermal lattice. The temperature of the three leftmost sites is set to vary sinusoidally as an excitation signal. (B) The temperature distribution of the localized mode in a H-SSH case (v1 = v2 < w), and the measured spatial profile of average temperature amplitudes normalized by the excitation signal amplitude. (C) The temperature distribution and spatial profile of the extended mode in a NH-SSH case (v1 < v2 = w).

sec.p: The equivalent thermal lattice of the expected model is shown in Fig. 2D, which can be called as a quasi-1D NH-SSH lattice. The thermal energy in each site is described by ρcVdTn,jAB/dt=Qn,jAB, where ρ, c, V, and Q, respectively, represent the density, heat capacity, volume, and the injected thermal power. The designed coupling relationship gives dTn,jA/dt=ω0Tn,j-1A-Tn,j+1A+v1Tn,j-1B-Tn,j+1B+wTn-1,j-1B-Tn-1,j+1B and dTn,jB/dt=ω0Tn,j-1B-Tn,j+1B+v2Tn,j-1A-Tn,j+1A+wTn+1,j-1A-Tn+1,j+1A. Then the reduced effective bulk Hamiltonian is:

where w0, v1, v2 and w are designed couplings illustrated in Fig. 2D. Clearly, the Hamiltonian is equivalent to Eq. 5 if ks is viewed as a constant. See SI Appendix, Supplementary Note 1 for the detailed Derivation. We then build the lattice using COMSOL Multiphysics® to demonstrate the performance of localized and delocalized topological states in thermal systems (Fig. 2E). The thermal lattice consists of 29 rings in the x direction, with each ring comprising a periodic array of 10 sites within the s dimension. All sites are set to satisfy the predesigned coupling relationship through programming the supplied energy of heat sources. We first show the temperature distribution of the topological edge state of the H-SSH case, where the coupling parameters are v1 = v2 = 0.005, w = 0.02 and w0 = 0.05. Obviously, the mode is localized at the boundary, as illustrated by the amplitude profile along x direction. Then the NH-SSH case is investigated as v2 is further tuned to be 0.02. We see that the topological zero mode is delocalized from the boundary and becomes an extended profile. In both cases, the excitation signal is applied at the leftmost 10 sites, defined as: T1,j=Tref+Tampsinjks-ω0′t, where the site index j = 1,2…,10, the wavenumber ks = 2 π/10, the circular frequency w0′ = 2sinks w0, the reference temperature Tref = 293 K, and the temperature amplitude Tamp = 10 K. The simulation results confirm the theoretical prediction, showing that the edge states are real-valued and long-time survival. This can be reflected from the wave-like temperature curves observed at the marked sites over time (the time period tp=2π/ω0′), as shown in the subfigures of Fig. 2E.

Next, we experimentally show a quasi-1D thermal lattice to validate the above findings. Our experimental lattice consists of an array of 9 × 3 blocks (Fig. 3A), where the three sites in each column are arranged under PBC in the s-direction, equivalent to a nine-site NH-SSH chain along the x direction. Each building unit comprises a piece of copper block with a temperature sensor sticked on top and a thermoelectrical cooler (TEC) attached underneath to supply thermal power. The hopping between sites is achieved through the programmed thermal power controlled by driving voltage, processed based on the real-time monitored temperature returned from the sensors (see details in Materials and Methods). Since the programmable couplings are determined by setting coefficients without dependence on physical real space, applying PBC in our platform is straightforward. We set a sine-wave variation in temperature on the leftmost column (with a phase difference of 2 π/3 between every two adjacent sites), acting as a signal source. We first measure the topological edge mode of the H-SSH model with hoppings set as v1 = v2 = 0.003, w = 0.012 and w0 = 0.05. The temperature distribution at a specific time is shown in Fig. 3B, where the localization at the left boundary can be observed. Next, we introduce the NH-SSH model with nonreciprocal hopping by letting v2 = 0.012 (other parameters remain the same) and measure the temperature distribution, see Fig. 3C. We can see that the topological zero mode is reconfigured as delocalized from the boundary and extended into the bulk. The spatial profile of the temperature amplitude of each column is also summarized in Fig. 3 B and C. These experimental results agree well with the theoretical predictions. See Movie S2 for the time evolution of the experimentally monitored topological modes.

The simulation and experiment demonstration highlight two intriguing features of delocalized topological states: isolated from the bulk in the spectrum and extended into the bulk in the wavefunction, which become particularly fascinating when applied to thermal systems. It suggests the possibility of manipulating or switching the mode distribution of temperature fluctuations, thereby implying the controllability of dynamically stable heat transfer.

Similarly, various topological lattices can be constructed in diffusion systems with the proposed strategy, e.g., the higher-order quadrupole insulator (33–35). The method can be naturally generalized to a thermal quadrupole to achieve topological corner states at real frequency. Given a quadrupole model in Fig. 4A, where vx1′ and vx2′ (vy1′ and vy2′) are the intracell nonreciprocal hopping terms for the x (y) direction, the corresponding quasi-2D lattice to equivalently realize it in a diffusion system is depicted in Fig. 4B. (The on-site energy term is omitted.) See SI Appendix, Supplementary Note 2 for details. Fig. 4C is the spectrum for a 9 × 9 lattice with v1x′ = v1y′ = 1 and wx′ = wy′ = 4. For the open lattice has an odd number of sites, there always exists one topological zero mode. Fig. 4D gives the corresponding wavefunctions under different non-Hermitian parameters: the corner mode is localized at the lower-left corner when v1x′ = v2x′ < wx′ and v1y′ = v2y′ < wy′ (blue); the mode is extended in the x direction when v1x′ < v2x′ = wx′ and v1y′ = v2y′ < wy′ (green); the mode is extended in both the x and y direction when v1x′ < v2x′ = wx′ and v1y′ < v2y′ = wy′ (red). Simulation results also confirm the stable existence of these topological states, where excitation is applied to the three sites at the lower-left column (black arrows). See Movie S3 for the time evolution of the topological zero modes.

caption.p: Localized and delocalized topological modes in a thermal quadrupole lattice. (A) Model of a 2D non-Hermitian quadrupole insulator. (B) The corresponding quasi-2D thermal quadrupole lattice. (C) Eigenspectra of the lattice under different non-Hermitian parameters vx2′ and vy2′, with the topological zero modes pinned at zero energy. (D) The wavefunctions of the topological states in the thermal quadrupole lattice: the localized corner mode (blue box); the extended mode in the x direction (green box); the extended mode in both the x and y direction (red box). The upper row shows the temperature distributions, and the lower row gives their corresponding spatial profile of the temperature amplitudes (normalized).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In conclusion, we have proposed a groundbreaking strategy to bridge the gap between wave and diffusion systems, establishing a paradigm for realizing stably dynamic transportation in the diffusion regime. The conversion from a diffusion system to a wave-like system is achieved through an introduced periodic dimension of real space, enabling the creation of the thermal counterparts analogous to various topological lattices. We experimentally realize an active thermal lattice and observe localized and delocalized topological zero modes. Moreover, the lattice is programmable with arbitrarily set coupling coefficients so that the topological phases and topological modes can be flexibly switched. The platform is also potential to explore various non-Hermitian paradigms, such as parity-time symmetry (36), chiral topological states (37) and non-Hermitian gauge field (38). Our work highlights the possibility of diffusion systems as platforms for observing topological phenomena and opens avenues for the development of topological mode engineering in diverse diffusion applications.

sec.title: Numerical Simulations.
sec.p: To validate our findings, we build corresponding models using COMSOL Multiphysics®. The thermal lattice is comprised of an array of copper blocks with density ρ = 8,820 kg m−3 and heat capacity c = 420 J kg−1 K−1. For each block, a domain probe is defined on the surface to monitor real-time temperature. Meanwhile, each block is equipped with an internal heat source to supply thermal power, which is set as a function with respect to the temperature of neighboring sites, allowing us to realize the hopping relationship between sites within the thermal lattice. The temperature boundary conditions of the sites at the leftmost column are defined as time-dependent sine-wave functions to excite the topological zero modes. All other boundaries are thermally insulated. Additionally, if the initial condition of temperature distribution is closer to that of the desired mode in theory, less time is needed to reach the resonant steady state.

sec.title: Experiments.
sec.p: The experimental setup that realizes the quasi-1D NH-SSH thermal lattice is shown in Fig. 3A. Each site consists of a copper block (40 mm × 40 mm × 2 mm), a customized TEC, and a heat sink with circulating water, arranged from top to bottom. The hopping between sites within the thermal lattice is realized through the real-time control of instantaneous power injected into each copper block, computed based on the monitored temperature returned from the sensors positioned on the surface of each block. The underlying TECs facilitate real-time controllable power, providing heating/cooling power for the corresponding sites through the input voltage, governed by the following equations:

where U and I is the input voltage and current, respectively. The three representative parameters of a TEC are: α—Seebeck coefficient, R—electrical resistance, and κt—thermal conductance. These parameters are retrieved from the data of test experiments. Tupper and Tlower are the temperature of the upper and lower surfaces of the TEC, which are measured in real time by built-in thermistor sensors. We use a water-cooling system that can effectively moderate the temperature fluctuations of the TEC lower surfaces and thus beneficial to the controllability of the thermal power. Note that Q>0 (Q<0) means a heating (cooling) power, and I>0 (I<0) stands for the heating (cooling) mode of the TEC. The experimental setup makes the tight binding approximation applicable, for the copper blocks are highly conductive and in full contact with the active sources, so that the temperature within each block can be considered uniform without any significant gradient.

The embedded controller utilizes a 32-bit microcontroller chip based on Cortex-M3 kernel from STMicroelectronics, responsible for collecting temperature data and controlling the driving voltage. The electrical voltage supplied to each TEC is manipulated via pulse width modulation (PWM). As a result, real-time adjustable thermal power is achieved by tuning the duty cycle of the PWM voltage, guaranteeing the desired hoppings among sites. Additionally, it provides the capability to generate temperature signals with different amplitudes and frequencies, such as the sinusoidal wave used as the excitation signal.

For the experimental results, the temperature of the leftmost column is defined as: Tn=1,j=1,2,3=Tref+Tampsinjks-ω0′t, where ks = 2 π/3, w0′ = 2sinks w0, w0 = 0.05, Tref = 293 K, and Tamp = 10 K. Interfaces between blocks and TECs are filled with thermal grease (thermal conductivity > 7 W m−1 K−1) for efficient conduction. To facilitate the rapid attainment of a dynamically stable state in the thermal lattice, we first generate an initial temperature that closely approximates that of the theoretical topological mode. Then the remaining sites evolve with time according to the established coupling relationships. The evolution of temperature profiles is measured with an infrared camera (Fotric 287+). We give the measured spatial profile of the temperature amplitudes of the states by averaging the temperature amplitudes of the three sites in every column over eight time periods. The dominant source of error is the accuracy of thermal power, which can be optimized by calibrating the parameters of TECs. Other errors come from the discrete time step, the accuracy of temperature sensors, and so on. Despite the imperfectness leading to slight discrepancy between simulations and experiments, the existence of the edge states is guaranteed by the topological protection.

Time evolution of the topological states in a quasi-2D thermal quadrupole lattice, exhibiting a corner mode, an x-extended mode, and an x & y-extended mode under varying non-Hermitian parameters.
